## PassThrough configuration

The PrimeVue-backed components use Vue's *PassThrough* (PT) pattern for fine-grained styling. Each component accepts a `pt` prop in addition to the schema above — for the full PrimeVue PassThrough API, see the [PrimeVue documentation](https://primevue.org/theming/#passthrough){rel="&#x22;nofollow&#x22;"}.

```ts [Customising a data-table's PassThrough]
import DataTableComponent from '@genicul-primevue/registry/components/data-table.vue';

const table = DataTableComponent as unknown as { __pt?: unknown };
// PassThrough is configured at mount time via the PrimeVue <PrimeVue> provider;
// the registry components inherit those defaults unless overridden.
```

::note
PassThrough customization is framework-level (PrimeVue), not a GenicUI surface. GenicUI does not pass an explicit 

`pt`

 object — applications customize it at the PrimeVue provider level.
::

## Trust boundary

Every prop schema above is `additionalProperties: false`. The server-side catalog rejects any prop that is not enumerated; the client-side component never receives unexpected keys. This is the trust boundary in action — see [Concepts → Trust Boundary](https://genicui.vaah.ai/concepts/trust-boundary).

If you add a prop to a component, you must:

1. Add it to `propsSchema.properties` in `registries/primevue/registry.json`.
2. Update the Vue component to read it.
3. Update the matching TypeBox schema in `packages/server/src/mcp/catalog.ts` (server-side validator).
4. Bump the component `version` field in `registry.json`.


# Custom Auth Wrapping

Replace the built-in API-key check with a JWT, OAuth, or mTLS validator. The GenicUI server exposes `wrapWithValidation()` for exactly this — insert your auth middleware ahead of the trust-boundary pipeline so a bad token never reaches `stripProtoKeys`.

## Problem

You need to authenticate agents against your existing identity provider (Auth0, Clerk, AWS Cognito, internal OAuth). The shipped API-key path (`X-API-Key: gnc_live_…`) is great for service-to-service but doesn't satisfy an enterprise customer's SAML/JWT requirement.

## Solution

Run your token validation in front of the server's tool handlers. The trust boundary (`stripProtoKeys` → `Value.Check`) only runs after your auth middleware returns 200; rejected tokens short-circuit with the standard `-32007 auth_invalid` JSON-RPC code.

::callout{type="info"}
The auth check runs in step 

**0**

 of the pipeline — see 

[Trust Boundary › The input validation pipeline](https://genicui.vaah.ai/concepts/trust-boundary#the-input-validation-pipeline)

. A failure here never reaches step 1, so you can't accidentally pollute the idempotency cache with an invalid payload.
::

## Code

```ts [packages/server/src/auth/jwt-middleware.ts]
import { jwtVerify, createRemoteJWKSet } from 'jose';
import type { Middleware } from './middleware.js'; // local middleware type

const JWKS = createRemoteJWKSet(new URL(process.env.JWT_JWKS_URL!));

export const jwtAuth: Middleware = async (req, next) => {
  const header = req.headers.get('authorization') ?? '';
  const token = header.replace(/^Bearer\s+/i, '');
  if (!token) {
    return Response.json({ error: 'missing_token' }, { status: 401 });
  }
  try {
    const { payload } = await jwtVerify(token, JWKS, {
      issuer: process.env.JWT_ISSUER,
      audience: 'genicui-server',
    });
    // Attach the verified subject so handlers can scope per-user state
    (req as any).auth = { sub: payload.sub, scope: payload.scope };
    return next(req);
  } catch (err) {
    return Response.json({ error: 'invalid_token' }, { status: 401 });
  }
};
```

Wire it into the server's middleware chain before `wrapWithValidation()`:

```ts [packages/server/src/index.ts]
import { jwtAuth } from './auth/jwt-middleware.js';

export function createServer(): Elysia {
  return new Elysia()
    .use(jwtAuth)                          // ← runs first
    .use(wrapWithValidation())             // ← trust boundary
    .mount('/mcp', mcpRouter)
    .mount('/ws', wsRouter);
}
```

## Verification

```bash
# 1. Boot the server with the JWKS URL set
JWT_JWKS_URL=https://your-idp.example.com/.well-known/jwks.json \
JWT_ISSUER=https://your-idp.example.com/ \
bun packages/server/bin/start.ts

# 2. Send an authenticated tool call with a valid JWT
TOKEN=$(your-idp-cli issue --aud genicui-server)
curl -X POST http://localhost:3040/mcp \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":"1","method":"tools/list"}'
# expect: 200 OK with the tool catalog

# 3. Send the same call with a bad token
curl -X POST http://localhost:3040/mcp \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer not.a.real.jwt" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":"1","method":"tools/list"}'
# expect: 401 with { "error": "invalid_token" }
```

A 401 on step 3 confirms the trust boundary never ran. If you see `-32003 props_invalid` after step 3, your middleware is wired *after* `wrapWithValidation()` — swap the order.

## Pitfalls

- **Don't trust the body.** Auth must read the `Authorization` header only. A request body containing `"apiKey": "gnc_live_…"` is just data — `wrapWithValidation()` would otherwise process it as props.
- **Cache the JWKS.** `createRemoteJWKSet()` already does this, but if you write your own key resolver, cache the keyset with a 10-minute TTL — hammering your IdP on every request is a denial-of-service vector against yourself.
- **Set `clockTolerance` to 30s.** Clock drift between the agent host and the IdP is the #1 cause of spurious `-32007 auth_invalid` errors. `jose` accepts `clockTolerance: 30` in the verify options.
- **Forward the scope.** If your IdP issues scopes (`payload.scope`), attach them to `req.auth` and reject at the tool layer with `-32007` when a token lacks the required scope. Don't bake scope checks into the middleware — they belong next to the tool definition.
- **Never log the token.** F46 ships a log scrubber that redacts known patterns; your custom middleware must add the token prefix (`Bearer `+ first 8 chars) to the scrub list. Otherwise a `console.log(req.headers)` will leak credentials.

## Related

- [Concepts → Trust Boundary](https://genicui.vaah.ai/concepts/trust-boundary) — pipeline order, drop-vs-reject semantics, prototype-pollution strip.
- [API Reference → Server](https://genicui.vaah.ai/api/server#error-codes) — the full `-32001..-32010` namespace including `-32007 auth_invalid`.
- [API Reference → Agent Bridge → `LLMProviderConfig.headers`](https://genicui.vaah.ai/api/agent-bridge#llmproviderconfig) — pass the JWT to upstream LLM calls when your IdP requires it.


# Retry, Backoff, and Idempotency

Your agent's `render_component` call timed out. Was it mounted or not? Without idempotency, a retry double-mounts; with it, the second call returns the same `componentId` from the server's 24h LRU cache. This recipe shows the client-side retry loop that survives network flakes without producing duplicate components.

## Problem

Agents retry on every transient failure — Claude Code's MCP wrapper retries on timeouts and 5xx responses by default. A naive retry of `render_component` allocates a fresh `componentId` and renders the component twice. The user sees a flash of the old UI, then the new one replaces it.

## Solution

Two layers of defense:

1. **Idempotency key** (`idempotencyKey` / `clientRequestId`) — the server caches the response for 24h keyed by `(apiKey, idempotencyKey)`. A retry with the same key returns the original response.
2. **Exponential backoff with jitter** — the client waits 1s, 2s, 4s, 8s (capped at 30s) with ±25% jitter between attempts. After 5 attempts, dead-letter the call.

::callout{type="info"}
The 24h TTL is enforced by an LRU cache. See 

[Frames › Idempotency keys](https://genicui.vaah.ai/concepts/frames#idempotency-keys)

 for the cache key shape and the silent-eviction policy.
::

## Code

```ts [lib/retry.ts]
import { randomUUID } from 'node:crypto';

type RetryOpts = {
  maxAttempts?: number;     // default 5
  baseMs?: number;          // default 1_000
  capMs?: number;           // default 30_000
  jitter?: number;          // default 0.25 (±25%)
};

const TRANSIENT = new Set([408, 425, 429, 500, 502, 503, 504, 1013]);

export async function withRetry<T>(
  fn: (key: string) => Promise<T>,
  opts: RetryOpts = {},
): Promise<T> {
  const { maxAttempts = 5, baseMs = 1_000, capMs = 30_000, jitter = 0.25 } = opts;
  // Stable per-call-site key — reused across retries
  const idempotencyKey = randomUUID();
  let lastErr: unknown;
  for (let attempt = 1; attempt <= maxAttempts; attempt++) {
    try {
      return await fn(idempotencyKey);
    } catch (err: any) {
      lastErr = err;
      const status = err?.status ?? err?.code;
      const retryable = TRANSIENT.has(status) || err?.name === 'AbortError';
      if (!retryable || attempt === maxAttempts) throw err;
      const backoff = Math.min(baseMs * 2 ** (attempt - 1), capMs);
      const wait = backoff * (1 + (Math.random() * 2 - 1) * jitter);
      await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, wait));
    }
  }
  throw lastErr;
}
```

Use it for every tool call that mutates state:

```ts [lib/render.ts]
import { withRetry } from './retry.js';
import { callTool } from './mcp-client.js';

export const renderDataTable = (props: Record<string, unknown>) =>
  withRetry((key) =>
    callTool('render_component', {
      name: 'DataTable',
      props,
      idempotencyKey: key,   // ← same key on every retry
    }),
  );
```

## Verification

Send 5 identical requests with the same `idempotencyKey` and confirm the server mounts exactly once:

```bash
KEY=$(uuidgen)
for i in 1 2 3 4 5; do
  curl -s -X POST http://localhost:3040/mcp \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $GENICUI_API_KEY" \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d "{\"jsonrpc\":\"2.0\",\"id\":\"$i\",\"method\":\"tools/call\",\"params\":{\"name\":\"render_component\",\"arguments\":{\"name\":\"DataTable\",\"props\":{\"rows\":[]},\"idempotencyKey\":\"$KEY\"}}}"
done

# All five responses should share the same componentId, e.g.:
# {"componentId":"dt-sess9f8e-01HK9X"}
```

The server log will show exactly one `STATE_SNAPSHOT` and one `COMPONENT_MOUNTED` emission. If you see five mounts, your retry layer is generating a fresh key per attempt — check `withRetry`.

## Pitfalls

- **Don't reuse keys across `render` vs `update`.** A `render_component` key and a later `update_component` call sharing the same key collide — the server sees a `params` mismatch and returns `-32007 idempotency_conflict`. Use the same key *only* across retries of the same logical operation.
- **Keys expire after 24h.** A user who retries a render that succeeded yesterday gets a fresh mount and a second `componentId`. Persist `(componentId, idempotencyKey)` pairs in your session store if you need to survive TTL eviction.
- **Backoff cap of 30s matches the server.** The runtime's reconnect loop also uses 30s as its cap ([Events › Backpressure](https://genicui.vaah.ai/concepts/events#backpressure-and-rate-limits)). Capping client-side backoff higher just makes you look hung to the user.
- **Dead-letter, don't silently drop.** After `maxAttempts`, persist the failed call to a queue (Redis Streams, SQS, a local SQLite). Surface it in your agent's UI as "1 retryable failure, click to retry" — silent drops are how users lose trust.
- **Don't retry `-32003 props_invalid`.** Validation errors are deterministic — retrying won't fix them. Add `400` to the non-retryable list (it's not in `TRANSIENT` above) and surface the error to the user.
- **Skip the retry for `401`/`403`.** Token expiry needs a refresh, not a backoff. Catch `err.status === 401` separately, refresh the token, then retry *once* with the new bearer.

## Related

- [Concepts → Frames › Idempotency keys](https://genicui.vaah.ai/concepts/frames#idempotency-keys) — cache key shape, 24h LRU, silent eviction.
- [API Reference → Server › `update_component`](https://genicui.vaah.ai/api/server#update_component) — JSON-Patch + merge modes, `-32004 patch_invalid`.
- [API Reference → Server › Error codes](https://genicui.vaah.ai/api/server#error-codes) — full error namespace including `-32007 idempotency_conflict`.


# Custom Event Types

Out of the box, `GenicElement` propagates click-style events. But what about drag, hover, focus, swipe, and any other pointer mutation you want to send to the agent? This recipe adds a custom event surface — emit it correctly, debounce the noise, and bound the payload.

## Problem

You want to track rich pointer state on a `<genic-data-table>` row — `drag_started`, `drag_ended`, `hover_changed`, `focus_changed` — not just `row_selected`. The default `row_selected` event fires once per click; a drag-tracked UI fires hundreds of `drag_over` events per second.

## Solution

Subclass `GenicElement`, attach pointer listeners, dispatch `CustomEvent` with `composed: true` so it crosses the closed Shadow DOM, declare each new event in `static events` with a TypeBox `payloadSchema`, and debounce the high-frequency ones at the source.

::callout{type="warning"}
Events without 

`composed: true`

 are silently dropped at the Shadow boundary — see 

[Events › The composed: true decision](https://genicui.vaah.ai/concepts/events#the-composed-true-decision)

. F19-AC1 enforces this.
::

## Code

```ts [src/genui/components/drag-row-table.ts]
import { GenicElement } from '@genicui/client';
import { Type, type Static } from '@sinclair/typebox';

const DragRowEvents = {
  drag_started: Type.Object({
    rowId: Type.String(),
    x: Type.Number(),
    y: Type.Number(),
  }, { additionalProperties: false }),

  drag_ended: Type.Object({
    rowId: Type.String(),
    droppedOn: Type.Union([Type.String(), Type.Null()]),
  }, { additionalProperties: false }),

  hover_changed: Type.Object({
    rowId: Type.Union([Type.String(), Type.Null()]),
  }, { additionalProperties: false }),

  focus_changed: Type.Object({
    rowId: Type.String(),
    focused: Type.Boolean(),
  }, { additionalProperties: false }),
};

type DragRowEvents = Static<typeof DragRowEvents>;

export class DragRowTable extends GenicElement {
  static events = DragRowEvents;

  connectedCallback() {
    super.connectedCallback();
    this.addEventListener('pointerdown', this.onDown);
    this.addEventListener('pointermove', this.onMove);
    this.addEventListener('pointerup', this.onUp);
    this.addEventListener('pointerenter', this.onEnter);
    this.addEventListener('pointerleave', this.onLeave);
  }

  disconnectedCallback() {
    super.disconnectedCallback();
    this.removeEventListener('pointerdown', this.onDown);
    this.removeEventListener('pointermove', this.onMove);
    this.removeEventListener('pointerup', this.onUp);
    this.removeEventListener('pointerenter', this.onEnter);
    this.removeEventListener('pointerleave', this.onLeave);
  }

  // Debounce hover events — 200ms coalesce window
  private hoverTimer: ReturnType<typeof setTimeout> | null = null;
  private emitHover(rowId: string | null) {
    if (this.hoverTimer) clearTimeout(this.hoverTimer);
    this.hoverTimer = setTimeout(() => {
      this.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent('hover_changed', {
        detail: { rowId },
        bubbles: true,
        composed: true,
      }));
    }, 200);
  }

  private onDown = (e: PointerEvent) => {
    const row = (e.target as HTMLElement).closest('[data-row-id]');
    if (!row) return;
    const rowId = row.getAttribute('data-row-id')!;
    this.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent('drag_started', {
      detail: { rowId, x: e.clientX, y: e.clientY },
      bubbles: true, composed: true,
    }));
  };

  private onMove = (e: PointerEvent) => {
    // pointermove fires 100s/sec — debounce or batch
    this.emitHover((e.target as HTMLElement).closest('[data-row-id]')?.getAttribute('data-row-id') ?? null);
  };

  private onUp = (e: PointerEvent) => {
    const row = (e.target as HTMLElement).closest('[data-row-id]');
    const droppedOn = row?.getAttribute('data-row-id') ?? null;
    this.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent('drag_ended', {
      detail: { rowId: droppedOn ?? 'unknown', droppedOn },
      bubbles: true, composed: true,
    }));
  };

  private onEnter = (e: PointerEvent) =>
    this.emitHover((e.target as HTMLElement).closest('[data-row-id]')?.getAttribute('data-row-id') ?? null);

  private onLeave = () => this.emitHover(null);
}

customElements.define('genui-drag-row-table', DragRowTable);
```

## Verification

```bash
# 1. Mount the component
curl -X POST http://localhost:3040/mcp \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $GENICUI_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":"1","method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"render_component","arguments":{"name":"DragRowTable","props":{"rows":[{"id":"r1"},{"id":"r2"}]}}}}'
# → returns componentId, e.g. drt-sess9f8e-01HK9X

# 2. Subscribe to the new events
curl -X POST http://localhost:3040/mcp \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $GENICUI_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":"2","method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"subscribe_to_events","arguments":{"componentId":"drt-sess9f8e-01HK9X","actions":["drag_started","drag_ended","hover_changed"]}}}'

# 3. Open the playground and drag a row across the table.
# The WebSocket on the server emits (in order):
#   drag_started  { rowId: "r1", x: 142, y: 318 }
#   hover_changed { rowId: "r2" }            ← only after 200ms quiet
#   drag_ended    { rowId: "r2", droppedOn: "r2" }
```

The verification proves three things: the events cross the Shadow boundary (`composed: true`), the server's `payloadSchema` validation accepts them, and the 200ms debounce coalesces the pointermove storm into a single wire frame.

## Pitfalls

- **Debounce at the source.** Server-side throttling caps at 200 events/sec per component ([Events › Backpressure](https://genicui.vaah.ai/concepts/events#backpressure-and-rate-limits)) — drag fires faster than that. If you don't debounce, the server drops the tail of the stream and `drop_count` ticks up silently.
- **Bound the payload.** A `drag_started` event with the full row tree (`detail: { row }`) couples your schema to your UI tree. Send only the `rowId` — let the agent `update_component` to fetch the row's current state if it needs more.
- **Don't dispatch `focus_changed` on every focus movement.** Browser focus events fire on tab, on click, on programmatic `element.focus()` — your agent will see noise. Emit on `blur` of the *previous* element + `focus` of the new one, or skip `focus_changed` entirely and let the agent rely on `selection`.
- **`composed: true` is non-negotiable.** See the callout above — events without it never leave the Shadow DOM. The runtime's event bridge listens at `document` with `{ capture: true }`; without the flag, the event stops at the Shadow Root.
- **Validate `payloadSchema`.** Each entry in `static events` is read by the trust boundary when the server validates the inbound event. An undeclared event name returns a warning and increments `drop_count`. Add every event you emit.
- **Cleanup listeners on `disconnectedCallback`.** Pointer listeners attached in `connectedCallback` leak if not removed. The example above pairs each `addEventListener` with a matching `removeEventListener`.

## Related

- [Concepts → Events](https://genicui.vaah.ai/concepts/events) — `composed: true`, `subscribe_to_events` filtering, end-to-end event flow.
- [API Reference → Client › `GenicElement`](https://genicui.vaah.ai/api/client#genicelement) — base class, observed attributes, lifecycle hooks.
- [API Reference → Server › `subscribe_to_events`](https://genicui.vaah.ai/api/server#subscribe_to_events) — input schema, `actions[]` filter, auto-cleanup.


# Multi-Channel Coordination

A single WebSocket carries up to 256 channels — one per mounted component plus the three reserved system channels. When you need components to talk to each other (master → child, dashboard tiles syncing, multi-pane forms), use the `__broadcast__` channel as the coordination layer and a per-component channel for state.

## Problem

You're rendering a dashboard with three tiles — a master filter, a summary card, and a detail table. When the user changes a filter on the master, the other two must update atomically. Each component already has its own channel for `STATE_SNAPSHOT`/`STATE_DELTA`. How do they coordinate without a separate RPC?

## Solution

Reserve `__broadcast__` (one of the three reserved channels) for cross-component coordination events. Components subscribe to `__broadcast__` and react to typed coordination frames. Each component's own channel still carries its `STATE_DELTA` — `__broadcast__` carries only the *coordination intent*, not the state.

::callout{type="warning"}
The three reserved channels — 

`__session__`

, 

`__mcp__`

, 

`__agent__`

 — are checked at mount time (

[Frames › Channel model](https://genicui.vaah.ai/concepts/frames#channel-model)

). Reusing them as component channels returns 

`-32008 surface_unavailable`

. 

`__broadcast__`

 is the 

*fourth*

 implicit reserved channel for cross-component events.
::

## Code

```ts [src/genui/components/dashboard-master.ts]
import { GenicElement } from '@genicui/client';
import { envelope } from '@genicui/core';

export class DashboardMaster extends GenicElement {
  static events = {
    filter_changed: /* schema */ undefined as never,
  };

  // The runtime injects a bridge with .send(channel, frame)
  private bridge = GenicElement.getRuntimeBridge();

  private onFilterChange = (e: Event) => {
    const value = (e.target as HTMLInputElement).value;
    // 1. Update own state via normal STATE_DELTA path
    this.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent('filter_changed', {
      detail: { value }, bubbles: true, composed: true,
    }));

    // 2. Coordinate with siblings via __broadcast__
    this.bridge.send('__broadcast__', envelope(
      'COORDINATION',
      {
        kind: 'filter.changed',
        source: this.componentId,
        payload: { value },
      },
      '__broadcast__',
    ));
  };

  connectedCallback() {
    super.connectedCallback();
    this.addEventListener('change', this.onFilterChange);
  }
}

customElements.define('genui-dashboard-master', DashboardMaster);
```

Child components subscribe to `__broadcast__` and apply the coordination:

```ts [src/genui/components/dashboard-detail.ts]
import { GenicElement } from '@genicui/client';

export class DashboardDetail extends GenicElement {
  connectedCallback() {
    super.connectedCallback();
    GenicElement.getRuntimeBridge().onEvent((evt) => {
      if (evt.kind === 'COORDINATION' && evt.detail?.kind === 'filter.changed') {
        // Apply the filter to own state — runtime will emit STATE_DELTA
        this.setAttribute(
          'props-json',
          JSON.stringify({ ...this.props, filter: evt.detail.payload.value }),
        );
      }
    });
  }
}

customElements.define('genui-dashboard-detail', DashboardDetail);
```

The agent observes the resulting frame sequence:

```text
__broadcast__: COORDINATION { kind: 'filter.changed', source: 'master-id' }
master channel:  STATE_DELTA { patch: [{op: 'replace', path: '/filter', value: 'active'}] }
detail channel:  STATE_DELTA { patch: [{op: 'replace', path: '/filter', value: 'active'}] }
summary channel: STATE_DELTA { patch: [{op: 'replace', path: '/count',   value: 42}] }
```

All four frames are causally consistent — the `__broadcast__` frame arrives before any sibling `STATE_DELTA`, so the agent's next tool call sees the post-filter state on every component.

## Verification

```bash
# 1. Render three components
for name in DashboardMaster DashboardDetail DashboardSummary; do
  curl -s -X POST http://localhost:3040/mcp \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $GENICUI_API_KEY" \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d "{\"jsonrpc\":\"2.0\",\"id\":\"$name\",\"method\":\"tools/call\",\"params\":{\"name\":\"render_component\",\"arguments\":{\"name\":\"$name\",\"props\":{}}}}"
done
# → three componentIds

# 2. Open the playground. Change the filter on the master.
# The WebSocket inspector shows (in seq order):
#   channel=__broadcast__       type=COORDINATION       payload.kind=filter.changed
#   channel=<master-id>        type=STATE_DELTA        patch=[...filter...]
#   channel=<detail-id>        type=STATE_DELTA        patch=[...filter...]
#   channel=<summary-id>       type=STATE_DELTA        patch=[...count...]

# 3. Confirm the 256-channel cap is not breached. With three components,
# the server has reserved 4 channels (__session__, __mcp__, __agent__,
# __broadcast__) + 3 component channels = 7. You're well under cap.
```

To prove the cap, mount a loop:

```ts
// Stress test: mount until -32001 component_not_found
for (let i = 0; i < 300; i++) {
  try {
    await client.callTool('render_component', { name: 'DataTable', props: { rows: [] } });
  } catch (err) {
    if (err.code === -32001) {
      console.log(`channel cap hit at ${i} mounts`); // expect ~252
      break;
    }
  }
}
```

## Pitfalls

- **256 channels per socket.** Hard cap — opening the 257th returns `-32001 component_not_found`. With 3 reserved system channels + `__broadcast__` you get 252 component channels in practice. If you need more, open a second socket.
- **Don't put state on `__broadcast__`.** Coordination events are *intents* — the actual state lives on each component's own channel. Putting props on `__broadcast__` creates a write race: two siblings updating `__broadcast__` simultaneously produce torn reads.
- **Backpressure on `__broadcast__` is global.** The 500-frame outbound cap ([Events › Backpressure](https://genicui.vaah.ai/concepts/events#backpressure-and-rate-limits)) is per-socket, not per-channel. A coordination storm on `__broadcast__` consumes the same budget as a chatty component. Throttle coordination events the same way you'd throttle any high-frequency frame.
- **`envelope()` validates the channel name.** Passing `__broadcast__` as the third arg to `envelope()` is allowed because it's reserved — the validator checks against `RESERVED_CHANNELS`. If you mistype (`__boradcast__`), you get a `GenicUIError` before the frame hits the wire. See [Core API › `validateChannel`](https://genicui.vaah.ai/api/core#validatechannelchannel).
- **Don't subscribe on every render.** Attach the `onEvent` listener in `connectedCallback` and remove it in `disconnectedCallback`. The runtime guarantees the bridge is the same instance per socket, so adding listeners per-render leaks.
- **Causality over `causes[]`.** When the master dispatches a coordination frame, set `causes: [lastSeq]` on the `STATE_DELTA` so the agent's run-tracer can rebuild the causal chain. See [Protocol › Frame envelope schema](https://genicui.vaah.ai/concepts/protocol#frame-envelope-schema).

## Related

- [Concepts → Frames › Channel model](https://genicui.vaah.ai/concepts/frames#channel-model) — reserved channels, 256-channel cap, seq per channel.
- [Concepts → Protocol](https://genicui.vaah.ai/concepts/protocol) — `envelope()`, `causes[]`, the 14 AG-UI event types.
- [API Reference → Core › `validateChannel`](https://genicui.vaah.ai/api/core#validatechannelchannel) — reserved-channel check, error code.
- [API Reference → Core › `FrameBuffer`](https://genicui.vaah.ai/api/core#framebuffer) — replay buffer used by the session-recovery layer on reconnect.


# Registry Versioning and Coexistence

You depend on `@genicul-primevue/registry` but want to ship your own `DataTable` with custom props (e.g., a `csvExport` action your product team needs). Two registries now declare `DataTable`. Which wins?

## Problem

You ship an internal `@acme/data-table@2.0.0` to a customer who already has the official `@genicul-primevue/registry@1.0.0` installed. Both export a `DataTable` component. The agent's `find_ui_component` returns one; the other is invisible. Worse, the agent silently picks the "wrong" one and the customer's UI breaks.

## Solution

GenicUI loads registries from three tiers — **Project > User > Remote** — and the higher tier always wins. To force a specific version, pin it explicitly in your `registry.json` with a `version` constraint; the loader applies the pin *before* tier resolution, so a pin beats tier.

::callout{type="info"}
The default remote allow-list is 

`@genicul-primevue/registry`

 only. Other remote entries are dropped with a log warning. See 

[Registries › Trust tiers and resolution order](https://genicui.vaah.ai/concepts/registries#trust-tiers-and-resolution-order)

.
::

## Code

Pin a specific version in your project-level `registry.json`:

```json [registry.json — project tier]
{
  "id": "@acme/data-table",
  "version": "2.0.0",
  "trustTier": "project",
  "components": ["DataTable"],
  "pin": {
    "DataTable": {
      "registry": "@acme/data-table",
      "version": "2.0.0",
      "reason": "Internal-only DataTable with csvExport action."
    }
  }
}
```

Install both registries and let the loader resolve the conflict:

```bash
bun add @genicul-primevue/registry    # official, remote tier
bun add @acme/data-table              # internal, project tier
```

On boot, the loader walks each tier in order and applies your `pin`:

```text
[bootstrap] Loading registry "@acme/data-table@2.0.0" (project) — 1 component
[bootstrap] Loading registry "@genicul-primevue/registry@1.0.0" (remote) — 5 components
[bootstrap] Conflict on DataTable:
            project @acme/data-table@2.0.0   (pinned) ← winner
            remote  @genicul-primevue@1.0.0  (shadowed)
[bootstrap] Effective registry: 5 components (4 PrimeVue + 1 internal)
[bootstrap] WARNING: PrimeVue DataTable shadowed by pin. Set GENICUI_REGISTRY_DRY_RUN=1 to verify the pin before promoting.
```

To run the loader in dry-run mode and see the resolution *without* committing:

```bash
GENICUI_REGISTRY_DRY_RUN=1 bun packages/server/bin/start.ts
# The server prints the resolution matrix and exits without binding the port.
```

For coexisting registries where you want *both* available (different component names, no conflict), no pin is needed:

```text
@genicul-primevue/registry@1.0.0   → DataTable, InputPair, ResultCard, CityPicker, WeatherCard
@acme/charts@1.0.0                 → AreaChart, BarChart, PieChart
                                ─────
Effective registry                → 8 components (5 + 3, zero overlap)
```

## Verification

```bash
# 1. Install the conflicting pair
bun add @genicul-primevue/registry
bun add @acme/data-table

# 2. Dry-run the loader to verify resolution
GENICUI_REGISTRY_DRY_RUN=1 bun packages/server/bin/start.ts
# expect: PrimeVue DataTable shadowed, @acme/data-table@2.0.0 wins

# 3. Confirm via find_ui_component — only the pinned entry shows
curl -X POST http://localhost:3040/mcp \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $GENICUI_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":"1","method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"find_ui_component","arguments":{"query":"DataTable","topK":3}}}'
# expect: result lists ONLY @acme/data-table@2.0.0, no PrimeVue entry

# 4. Render and verify the schema matches the pinned component
curl -X POST http://localhost:3040/mcp \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $GENICUI_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":"2","method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"render_component","arguments":{"name":"DataTable","props":{"rows":[],"csvExport":true}}}}'
# expect: 200 OK; schema returned includes the csvExport prop
```

A schema-rejection on step 4 means the pin didn't take effect — your `registry.json` is in the wrong directory (project tier expects `./registry.json` at the workspace root) or the JSON is malformed.

## Pitfalls

- **Trust tier is silent.** No toast, no banner — the loader just resolves and moves on. If you shadow a third-party component by accident, the agent picks the wrong one with zero diagnostic. Always `GENICUI_REGISTRY_DRY_RUN=1` before promoting to production.
- **Pins are absolute.** A pinned component can't be temporarily overridden for one user or session. If you need per-tenant customization, build a *different* registry (e.g., `@acme/data-table-tenant-a`) and let the agent pick via `find_ui_component`'s `tags` filter — don't rely on tier resolution for per-user variations.
- **Bump the major on breaking schema changes.** The trust boundary rejects registries that change a `propsSchema`'s required keys without a major bump. See [Building a Custom Registry](https://genicui.vaah.ai/guides/custom-registry#publishing) — semver matters here because the schema check is strict.
- **Don't pin to `latest`.** A floating pin becomes a silent source of nondeterminism — your dev environment picks up the latest release, your staging picks up a different one. Always pin to an exact version (`2.0.0`, not `^2.0.0`).
- **Hot reload on `SIGHUP` only updates unpinned components.** A pinned entry is read once at boot; sending `SIGHUP` won't re-resolve the pin. Restart the server to pick up a new pinned version.
- **Two registries, one URI, different schemas** — never allow this in production. The loader throws at boot if the same `ui://` URI is claimed by two registries in the same tier. Move one to a different URI namespace (`ui://acme/...` vs `ui://genicul/...`).

## Related

- [Concepts → Registries](https://genicui.vaah.ai/concepts/registries) — `defineRegistry` contract, `ui://` URI grammar, three-tier resolution.
- [Guides → Building a Custom Registry](https://genicui.vaah.ai/guides/custom-registry) — the five-step process for authoring `@genicul-<yourlib>/registry` from scratch.
- [API Reference → PrimeVue Registry](https://genicui.vaah.ai/api/primevue-registry) — the canonical registry layout that your custom registry will mirror.


# Testing Components End-to-End

A full agent turn is render → update → event. Mocking all three is tempting — but mocking the trust boundary lets bugs through. This recipe runs the **real server** against an in-memory session and a stubbed LLM, then drives the Web Component half with Playwright. You get fast tests that catch what mocks miss.

## Problem

You want to assert that "clicking row #2 in `DataTable` emits a `row_selected` event with `{ rowId: '2' }` and the agent's next tool call is `update_component`." That's a render-update-event round trip. Pure unit tests can't see the WebSocket frames; full e2e with a real LLM is slow and flaky.

## Solution

Split the loop in two:

1. **Server half** (`agent → server → component`) — run the real GenicUI server against an `InMemoryStore`, use a stub LLM that returns a fixed tool-call sequence. Tests are deterministic and run in <500ms.
2. **Browser half** (`component → DOM → user`) — drive Playwright against `examples/playground/`, click rows, assert DOM mutations and outbound `CustomEvent`s.

::callout{type="info"}
The pattern below mirrors 

`examples/testing-cookbook/`

 — see 

[Testing › The pyramid](https://genicui.vaah.ai/guides/testing#the-pyramid)

 for the 150/20/3-5 split and where e2e sits.
::

## Code

Server half — in-process server with a stub LLM:

```ts [tests/integration/full-loop.test.ts]
import { test, expect } from 'bun:test';
import { createServer } from '@genicui/server';
import { InMemoryStore } from '@genicui/core';
import type { AgentBridge, LLMProvider } from '@genicui/agent-bridge';

// Stub LLM that returns a fixed tool-call sequence
const stubLLM: LLMProvider = {
  async chat(messages, tools) {
    return {
      choices: [{
        message: {
          role: 'assistant',
          tool_calls: [{
            id: 'tc-1',
            type: 'function',
            function: {
              name: 'render_component',
              arguments: JSON.stringify({
                name: 'DataTable',
                props: { rows: [{ id: '1' }, { id: '2' }], columns: [{ key: 'id', label: 'ID' }] },
              }),
            },
          }],
        },
      }],
    };
  },
};

test('agent renders DataTable, user clicks row #2, agent receives row_selected', async () => {
  // 1. Spin up the real server on an ephemeral port
  const app = createServer();
  const port = 3041;
  const server = app.listen(port);

  try {
    // 2. Open a WebSocket + call the stubbed agent
    const ws = new WebSocket(`ws://localhost:${port}/ws`);
    await new Promise((r) => ws.addEventListener('open', r, { once: true }));
    const bridge = await AgentBridge.connect(stubLLM, `http://localhost:${port}/mcp`);

    // 3. Drive the agent — first call renders, second emits a deterministic reply
    const reply = await bridge.execute('Show me a table');
    expect(reply).toBeTruthy();

    // 4. Simulate the user clicking row #2 on the open WebSocket
    const sent: any[] = [];
    ws.addEventListener('message', (e) => sent.push(JSON.parse(e.data)));
    ws.send(JSON.stringify({
      v: 1, channel: 'dt-...', type: 'COMPONENT_EVENT',
      payload: { componentId: 'dt-...', action: 'row_selected', detail: { rowId: '2' } },
      seq: 1,
    }));

    // 5. Assert the server forwarded to the agent subscription
    await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 50));
    expect(sent.some((f) => f.type === 'COMPONENT_EVENT' && f.payload?.detail?.rowId === '2'))
      .toBe(true);

    await bridge.close();
    ws.close();
  } finally {
    server.stop();
  }
});
```

Browser half — Playwright drives the Web Component:

```ts [e2e/click-row.spec.ts]
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('clicking a DataTable row dispatches row_selected with the row id', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('http://localhost:3042/');

  // Mount via MCP first (or use the playground's dev shortcut that mounts on load)
  await page.waitForSelector('genui-data-table');

  // Capture the composed CustomEvent
  const events: any[] = [];
  await page.exposeFunction('__captureEvent', (detail: unknown) => events.push(detail));
  await page.evaluate(() => {
    document.addEventListener('row_selected', (e: Event) =>
      (window as any).__captureEvent((e as CustomEvent).detail),
    { capture: true });
  });

  // Click the second row
  await page.locator('genui-data-table [data-row-id="2"]').click();

  // Assert the event crossed the Shadow boundary
  expect(events).toHaveLength(1);
  expect(events[0]).toEqual({ rowId: '2' });
});
```

## Verification

```bash
# 1. Run the server-half integration test
bun test tests/integration/full-loop.test.ts
# expect: 1 passed, ~400ms

# 2. Run the browser half
bunx playwright test e2e/click-row.spec.ts
# expect: 1 passed, ~3s

# 3. Full suite — proves the loop end-to-end
bun test && bunx playwright test e2e/
# expect: all green; the e2e layer catches what mocks miss (composed:true
# flag, attribute change timing, runtime bridge injection order)
```

If `bun test` fails on `createServer()`, check that you're not running it in parallel with another test that already holds port 3040. The pattern above uses 3041 explicitly; if you have multiple test files, pick a different port per file.

## Pitfalls

- **Don't mock the trust boundary.** The whole point of running the real server is that `stripProtoKeys` + `Value.Check` run on every call. A mocked boundary lets `-32003 props_invalid` through and your tests pass while prod breaks.
- **Use the real `InMemoryStore`, not Jest mocks.** `InMemoryStore` is the source-of-truth for session state during tests — Jest's `jest.fn()` mocks of `Map` miss edge cases (TTL eviction, `on('evicted')` callbacks). See [Core API › `InMemoryStore`](https://genicui.vaah.ai/api/core#inmemorystore).
- **Playwright `exposeFunction` is the right way to capture events.** Don't `console.log` from the page and parse stdout — that breaks when the page is sandboxed or the listener fires before Playwright attaches. Expose a function once and have the page call it.
- **Deterministic test data, not `Date.now()`.** The test pyramid's rule #4 ([Testing › Authoring rules](https://genicui.vaah.ai/guides/testing#authoring-rules)) — pass timestamps as fixtures. A test that asserts `subscription.expiresAt > Date.now()` fails intermittently.
- **Don't share ports across test files.** Bun's parallel runner will race. Pick a unique port per file (3041, 3042, 3043…) or set `GENICUI_PORT=0` and read the bound port from `server.address().port`.
- **Wire-format assertions > frame-content assertions.** Test that `STATE_DELTA` arrived, not that it arrived with exactly the patch ops you expected. The diff engine is allowed to coalesce `replace` ops into `add`/`remove` pairs without breaking the contract.

## Related

- [Concepts → Components](https://genicui.vaah.ai/concepts/components) — Web Component lifecycle, observed attributes, the runtime engine.
- [Guides → Testing](https://genicui.vaah.ai/guides/testing) — the 150/20/3-5 pyramid, property tests, conformance runner.
- [API Reference → Core › `InMemoryStore`](https://genicui.vaah.ai/api/core#inmemorystore) — `Map`-backed session store with eviction events.
- [API Reference → Client › `createRuntime`](https://genicui.vaah.ai/api/client#createruntimeoptions-and-runtimeengine) — the runtime engine the Playwright spec drives.


# Overview

Pick the host that matches your traffic profile, ops preference, and existing infrastructure. GenicUI ships the same `@genicui/server` runtime against four targets — three for the runtime, one for this doc site. This page is the decision matrix; the three option pages that follow (Cloudflare, Bun, Nitro) are landing pages linking to the M6 deep dives.

::callout{type="info"}
**Vercel hosts this doc site — it is not a runtime target for GenicUI itself.**

 The GenicUI runtime choices are Cloudflare Workers, Bun self-host, and the Nitro/Nuxt binding. If you're deploying GenicUI as a product, skip the Vercel column below and pick a runtime row.
::

## Decision matrix

| Target                                                                                   | Best for                        | Cold start           | State store                      | Setup effort                             | Trade-off                                            |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------- | -------------------- | -------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| **Cloudflare Workers + DO** ([deep dive](https://genicui.vaah.ai/deployment/cloudflare)) | Production, multi-region edge   | \~50ms (Workers p95) | Durable Objects SQLite (>1MB)    | Medium — `wrangler.toml` + DO migrations | 30s request limit, DO pricing, hibernation semantics |
| **Bun self-host** ([deep dive](https://genicui.vaah.ai/deployment/bun-self-host))        | Dev, CI, single-tenant, on-prem | 0ms (always warm)    | In-memory `Map` (MVP); pluggable | Trivial — `bun run start`                | You own ops, no auto-scaling, single-region          |
| **Nitro/Nuxt binding** ([deep dive](https://genicui.vaah.ai/deployment/nitro))           | Existing Nuxt apps              | Inherits host        | In-memory, host-store pluggable  | Easy — `pnpm add nuxt-genicui`           | Tied to Nuxt release cycle; can't run on Workers     |
| **Vercel (docs site only)**                                                              | This documentation site         | (static)             | (static, Git)                    | Trivial — Git push                       | Not for runtime; static SSG only                     |

::callout{type="warning"}
**Trade-offs matter more than features.**

 Each row's right column is what you 

*give up*

. Read it before committing to a target.
::

## Pick one

```text
Where will GenicUI run?
├── Multi-region edge in front of users?  → Cloudflare Workers + DO
├── One region, full control, on-prem?    → Bun self-host
└── Already running a Nuxt app?           → Nitro / Nuxt binding
```

If two of these apply (e.g. global + Nuxt), **pick the binding that wins on infrastructure you already operate** — the deeper the integration, the worse the second host performs.

## When the answer is none of these

Three signals point at a host not in the matrix:

- **Need Kubernetes** — wait for the Phase-3 work tracked in the [roadmap](https://genicui.vaah.ai/community/roadmap). Today there is no first-party `Deployment` manifest; community-maintained options live in the [community › contributing](https://genicui.vaah.ai/community/contributing) list.
- **Need a fully managed control plane** — same answer as above. Cloudflare's managed Durable Objects are the closest available; nothing else ships in the MVP.
- **Need to deploy the doc site somewhere other than Vercel** — see the [Vercel deploy guide](https://genicui.vaah.ai) — the project includes `vercel.json` and an opinionated `nitro` preset, but a Cloudflare Pages or Netlify drop-in is in scope for a follow-up.

## Next steps

- Cloudflare — [Workers + Durable Objects](https://genicui.vaah.ai/deployment/cloudflare), M6-T1 deep dive
- Bun — [self-host binary](https://genicui.vaah.ai/deployment/bun-self-host), M6-T2 deep dive
- Nitro — [Nuxt binding](https://genicui.vaah.ai/deployment/nitro), M6-T4 deep dive
- Read the [production checklist](https://genicui.vaah.ai/guides/production) before flipping DNS — the 10-item gate covers CORS, auth, observability, and rate-limit hooks that no deployment target handles for you.

## See also

- [Production guide](https://genicui.vaah.ai/guides/production) — the 10-item checklist (CORS, auth rotation, observability, persistent storage, TLS, rate limits).
- [Trust boundary](https://genicui.vaah.ai/concepts/trust-boundary) — why input validation matters regardless of host.
- [Registries](https://genicui.vaah.ai/concepts/registries) — how the registry trust tiers interact with `GENICUI_REGISTRY_ALLOWLIST` per host.


# Cloudflare Workers

Run GenicUI on Cloudflare's edge network. Cold start p95 ≤ 50ms across the 300+ POPs, state persisted in Durable Object SQLite, WebSocket hibernation keeps sessions alive across restarts. This is the production-grade target chosen for the MVP.

This page is a **landing** — it links to the M6-T1 deep dive that owns the wiring, tests, and operational tools. If you've already decided on Cloudflare, jump straight to the M6-T1 task file; otherwise read the [overview](https://genicui.vaah.ai/deployment/overview) first.

## Architecture

A single Worker handles `/health`, `/ws`, and `/mcp`. Each session maps to one Durable Object instance, identified by `sessionId`. State lives in the DO's SQLite storage (one row per session, mutated in transactions). The [WebSocket Hibernation API](https://developers.cloudflare.com/durable-objects/learning/websockets/){rel="&#x22;nofollow&#x22;"} keeps a connection alive across the DO's \~10s inactivity window without dropping the client.

```ts
import { mountGenicUIForWorkers, GenicSessionDO } from '@genicui/server/workers';

export { GenicSessionDO };

export default {
  async fetch(request: Request, env: Env, ctx: ExecutionContext) {
    return mountGenicUIForWorkers({ request, env, ctx, sessionDO: GenicSessionDO });
  },
};

interface Env {
  SESSION: DurableObjectNamespace;
  GENICUI_API_KEY: string;
  GENICUI_LOG_LEVEL: string;
  GENICUI_HEARTBEAT_MS: string;
}
```

::note
**Why a DO per session, not one DO for all sessions?**

 A single DO would serialize every WebSocket message across all users — defeating the point of edge deployment. Per-session DOs scale horizontally with users and let the runtime pick the closest POP.
::

## Prerequisites

- A Cloudflare account with Workers + Durable Objects enabled
- `wrangler` CLI — `bun install -g wrangler && wrangler login`
- A `gnc_live_<32>` API key — `openssl rand -hex 16`
- A registered DO class via `wrangler.toml` (see the deep-dive for the file)

## Quick links

- **Deep dive** — `.vaahagents/milestones-and-tasks/milestone-06-deployment/task-M6-T1-cloudflare-workers-deploy.md` (F61)
- **Spec** — `.vaahagents/requirements/specs/deployment.md` §"Target 1: Cloudflare Workers + Durable Objects"
- **Code** — `packages/server/src/adapters/workers/` (the `mountGenicUIForWorkers` adapter)
- **DO session store** — `.vaahagents/milestones-and-tasks/milestone-06-deployment/task-M6-T3-do-session-store.md` (F62b)
- **Smoke commands** — see `wrangler deploy` + `curl .../health` in the spec

## Trade-offs

::callout{type="warning"}
**What you give up by choosing Cloudflare Workers:**

- **30-second CPU limit per request.** Long-running inference loops must be split across multiple invocations or moved to [Queue consumers](https://developers.cloudflare.com/queues/){rel=""nofollow""}. Streaming responses work; blocking waits over \~25s do not.
- **No native TCP / arbitrary ports.** The HTTP and WebSocket surfaces are first-class; raw database connections require a Tunnel or HTTP shim. SQLite via DO storage is the supported path.
- **DO per-request billing.** DO requests are cheap individually, but high-cardinality session creation can add up. Use `wrangler tail` to monitor.
- **Hibernation semantics.** State is durable; in-process state (`let x = ...`) is not. Per-message handlers must rehydrate from `state.storage.sql` on every entry.
- **No filesystem.** Bundling must happen at build time. Dynamic `import()` of unsupported modules fails. The `nodejs_compat` flag covers most Node APIs.

If any of these is a hard blocker, the [Bun self-host](https://genicui.vaah.ai/deployment/bun-self-host) or [Nitro binding](https://genicui.vaah.ai/deployment/nitro) may be a better fit.
::

## Operational tooling

- `wrangler tail` — stream live Worker logs
- `wrangler secret put GENICUI_API_KEY` — rotate the API key without a redeploy
- `wrangler deploy --env production` — promote a built Worker
- DO inspector — list DO instances by ID from the Cloudflare dashboard

The [production checklist](https://genicui.vaah.ai/guides/production) covers the 10-item gate that applies *after* Cloudflare is wired (CORS, observability, log scrubbing, rate-limit hooks).

## See also

- [Deployment overview](https://genicui.vaah.ai/deployment/overview) — the decision matrix
- [Bun self-host](https://genicui.vaah.ai/deployment/bun-self-host) — escape hatch for hosts that can't run Workers
- [Nitro binding](https://genicui.vaah.ai/deployment/nitro) — when GenicUI is one feature of a larger Nuxt app
- [Production guide](https://genicui.vaah.ai/guides/production) — the post-deploy 10-item gate


# Bun Self-Host

Run GenicUI as a single OS binary with no external runtime install. Two paths share the same `@genicui/server/bun` adapter: `bun run start` for fast iteration, and `bun build --compile` for a static binary you can ship to bare hosts and containers.

This page is a **landing** — it links to the M6-T2 deep dive that owns the binary, sizing, and cold-start tests. If you've already decided on Bun, jump to the M6-T2 task file; otherwise skim the [overview](https://genicui.vaah.ai/deployment/overview) decision matrix first.

## When to pick Bun

Three signals point at self-host over Cloudflare:

- **You already operate servers.** You have a deploy target, an SSH / Ansible / systemd story, or a Kubernetes cluster — and you'd rather not introduce a third vendor.
- **One region is fine.** You're serving a single geography, an internal tool, or a backend service that isn't user-facing.
- **Dev and CI parity.** You want the local process to be the same artifact the test suite and CI smoke test exercise.

## Two ways to run

::tabs
  :::tabs-item{icon="i-lucide-terminal" label="Dev / iteration"}
  Run the source directly — fastest iteration loop, full HMR, no build step:

  ```bash
  bun install
  bun run start
  # Server running at http://localhost:8080
  ```

  The entry point wires `@genicui/server/bun` into an Elysia app:

  ```ts
  import { Elysia } from 'elysia';
  import { mountGenicUIForBun } from '@genicui/server/bun';

  const app = new Elysia()
    .get('/health', () => ({ status: 'ok' }))
    .use(mountGenicUIForBun({
      apiKey: process.env.GENICUI_API_KEY,
      port: Number(process.env.GENICUI_PORT ?? 8080),
    }))
    .listen({ port: 8080, hostname: '0.0.0.0' });
  ```
  :::
::

::tabs-item{icon="i-lucide-package" label="Compiled binary"}
Compile to a single binary — host with no Bun install, ship as a container artifact, drop into a Kubernetes pod:

```bash
bun build src/server.ts --compile --outfile genicul
./genicui
```

The target binary is self-contained: `oven/bun:1.2` and `node:alpine` base images both run it. For a minimal Dockerfile:

```dockerfile
FROM oven/bun:1.2
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json bun.lock ./
RUN bun install --frozen-lockfile
COPY . .
RUN bun build src/server.ts --compile --outfile /usr/local/bin/genicui
EXPOSE 8080
CMD ["genicui"]
```

\::
\::

## Prerequisites

- Bun `1.2` or newer — `curl -fsSL https://bun.sh/install | bash`
- For binary compilation, a Linux build host that matches your deploy target
- A `gnc_live_<32>` API key — `openssl rand -hex 16`
- A reverse proxy for TLS (Caddy, Nginx, or Traefik) — GenicUI speaks plain HTTP/WS behind the proxy

## Quick links

- **Deep dive** — `.vaahagents/milestones-and-tasks/milestone-06-deployment/task-M6-T2-bun-self-host.md` (F62)
- **Spec** — `.vaahagents/requirements/specs/deployment.md` §"Target 2: Bun Self-host"
- **Code** — `packages/server/src/adapters/bun/` (the `mountGenicUIForBun` adapter)
- **Adapter docs** — [Server › API Reference](https://genicui.vaah.ai/api/server) for the full options shape

## Trade-offs

  :::callout{type="warning"}
  **What you give up by choosing Bun self-host:**

  - **You own ops.** Process supervision, log shipping, secret rotation, OS patching, and capacity planning are on you. A `systemd` unit or a k8s `Deployment` is your job.
  - **No auto-scaling.** Horizontal scale is manual (or scripted) — add capacity before traffic spikes, not after.
  - **Single region by default.** Multi-region requires running the binary in N regions and putting a smart load balancer (or DNS-based geo) in front.
  - **In-memory state by default.** The MVP store loses sessions on restart. Wire [Postgres or SQLite](https://bun.sh/docs/api/sqlite){rel=""nofollow""} yourself, or accept the loss.
  - **Cold start = 0ms only because you're always warm.** If you autoscale to zero, the first request pays the boot cost. Cloudflare's hibernation model avoids this by design.

  If any of these is a hard blocker, the [Cloudflare Workers](https://genicui.vaah.ai/deployment/cloudflare) target or the [Nitro binding](https://genicui.vaah.ai/deployment/nitro) may be a better fit.
  :::

## Operational tooling

- `bun run start` — local iteration
- `bun build src/server.ts --compile --outfile genicul` — produce a binary
- `ls -lh genicul` — verify size budget (F62-AC2 requires <50MB)
- `systemctl status genicul` — process supervision
- `curl http://localhost:8080/health` — readiness probe

The [production checklist](https://genicui.vaah.ai/guides/production) covers the post-deploy gate (CORS, observability, log scrubbing, rate-limit hooks) that applies once your binary is behind a reverse proxy.

## See also

- [Deployment overview](https://genicui.vaah.ai/deployment/overview) — the decision matrix
- [Cloudflare Workers](https://genicui.vaah.ai/deployment/cloudflare) — when global + auto-scaling matter
- [Nitro binding](https://genicui.vaah.ai/deployment/nitro) — when GenicUI is one feature of a larger Nuxt app
- [Production guide](https://genicui.vaah.ai/guides/production) — the post-deploy 10-item gate
::


# Nitro / Nuxt Binding

Drop GenicUI into a Nuxt app as a first-class module. The `nuxt-genicui` module wires the same `@genicui/server` runtime into the host app at `/api/ws`, so GenicUI shares the host's origin, the host's auth middleware, and the host's infrastructure.

This page is a **landing** — it links to the M6-T4 deep dive that owns the module, the devtools panel, and the auth-from-env wiring. If you've already decided on a Nitro binding, jump to the M6-T4 task file; otherwise compare against the [overview](https://genicui.vaah.ai/deployment/overview) options.

## When to pick Nitro

Three signals point at the binding over a standalone target:

- **Nuxt is your primary app.** You're already deploying a Nuxt site — adding a second service means CORS, origin validation, and infrastructure duplication that the binding removes by construction.
- **Same-origin wins.** WebSocket upgrades don't require CORS when they share an origin with the page. The host app's auth middleware can gate the WS endpoint.
- **Shared observability.** Logs, traces, and request metrics stay in your existing aggregator. No second set of dashboards.

## Architecture

The module auto-generates a Nitro WebSocket handler at `server/api/ws.ts`. The handler delegates the WebSocket lifecycle to `@genicui/server/nitro`, which uses the same core runtime as the Workers and Bun adapters.

```ts
// nuxt.config.ts
export default defineNuxtConfig({
  modules: ['nuxt-genicui', '@genicui/client'],
  genicui: {
    apiKey: process.env.GENICUI_API_KEY, // read from env, never checked in
    surface: 'default',
  },
});
```

```ts
// auto-generated at build: server/api/ws.ts
import { mountGenicUIForNitro } from '@genicui/server/nitro';

export default defineWebSocketHandler({
  open(peer) {
    mountGenicUIForNitro({ peer, config: useRuntimeConfig().genicui });
  },
  message(peer, message) {
    // delegated to @genicui/server core
  },
  close(peer) {
    // cleanup
  },
});
```

::note
**Why same-origin matters for WebSocket.**

 Browsers refuse cross-origin WS upgrades without explicit permission (CORS doesn't apply to WS, but mixed-content and origin checks do). A same-origin 

`/api/ws`

 keeps your auth cookies and CSRF protections intact.
::

## Prerequisites

- Nuxt `3.x` or `4.x` with Nitro
- `pnpm add nuxt-genicui @genicui/server @genicui/client`
- A `gnc_live_<32>` API key in `GENICUI_API_KEY` (read via `process.env` at boot)
- Nitro's experimental WebSocket support enabled (default in Nitro ≥ 2.10)

## Quick links

- **Deep dive** — `.vaahagents/milestones-and-tasks/milestone-06-deployment/task-M6-T4-nuxt-binding.md` (F64)
- **Spec** — `.vaahagents/requirements/specs/deployment.md` §"Target 3: Nitro/Nuxt Binding"
- **Adapter code** — `packages/server/src/adapters/nitro/` (the `mountGenicUIForNitro` adapter)
- **Module code** — `packages/vite-plugin/` (the Vite/Nuxt build integration) and `examples/playground/` (a working Nitro host)

## Trade-offs

::callout{type="warning"}
**What you give up by choosing the Nitro binding:**

- **Tied to the Nuxt release cycle.** A Nuxt major version bump can require a `nuxt-genicui` release. The Workers and Bun adapters are decoupled from any framework's cadence.
- **Cannot run on Cloudflare Workers.** Nitro's WebSocket handler currently targets Node, Bun, and the Vercel/Netlify adapters. There is no Workers preset today.
- **Shared fate with the host app.** If the host app crashes, GenicUI goes down with it. Standalone deployments isolate failures better.
- **In-memory state by default.** Sessions live in the host process. For multi-instance Nuxt hosts you'll need a shared store (Postgres, Redis) — wire it yourself.
- **Devtools panel is part of the host UI.** F64-AC3 ships a sessions panel in `nuxt-devtools`. If you prefer a separate admin tool, the Cloudflare or Bun standalones expose a JSON admin API instead.

If any of these is a hard blocker, the [Cloudflare Workers](https://genicui.vaah.ai/deployment/cloudflare) target or the [Bun self-host](https://genicui.vaah.ai/deployment/bun-self-host) may be a better fit.
::

## Operational tooling

- `pnpm dev` — local Nuxt dev server with HMR for GenicUI components
- `pnpm build` — produce `.output/server` for any Nitro-compatible host (Vercel, Netlify, CF Pages, Node)
- `pnpm preview` — smoke-test the production bundle
- `nuxt-devtools` — GenicUI sessions panel lives under the Devtools tab

The [production checklist](https://genicui.vaah.ai/guides/production) covers the 10-item gate that applies *after* the Nuxt bundle ships (CORS, observability, log scrubbing, rate-limit hooks).

## See also

- [Deployment overview](https://genicui.vaah.ai/deployment/overview) — the decision matrix
- [Cloudflare Workers](https://genicui.vaah.ai/deployment/cloudflare) — for multi-region production
- [Bun self-host](https://genicui.vaah.ai/deployment/bun-self-host) — for hosts that can't run Nuxt
- [Production guide](https://genicui.vaah.ai/guides/production) — the post-deploy 10-item gate
